subtopic: SOCIAL AFFAIRS
SOCIAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: CALL FOR ASSESSMENT OF SOCIAL CHANGES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43. The 1981 census figures recently revealed dramatic social changes in Canada which will have powerful repercussions on Canada's economy and social fabric. For example, children under 15 years have decreased by 7 per cent, while persons over 65 years have increased by 17.9 per cent. Divorced persons have increased by 65 per cent, affecting half a million children. This means a tremendous increase in single parent families, a much larger pensioner group to be supported by fewer workers, and a huge increase in unemployed workers because of technological change. Inasmuch as the government develops long-range plans for energy resource development and for defence, but does no planning for human needs, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Nanaimo-Alberni (Mr. Miller):
That the government establish a parliamentary task force to assess the impact of these social changes and recommend long-range social policy directives to meet the future needs of Canadians.

subsubtopic: PROPOSED CHANGE OF SALES TAX TO WHOLESALE LEVEL
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Finance. After analysing the draft legislation on the proposed shift of the federal sales tax to the wholesale level, the Retail Council of Canada has calculated that prices on commodities that are
Oral Questions
affected will increase from 2 per cent to 6 per cent in addition to the normal inflationary increase. This is just simply as a result of the shift of the tax.
In face of the widespread concern about inflation as expressed in the record low level of consumer confidence that was announced this morning, why is the minister persisting in his pursuit of this shift in federal sales tax to the wholesale level?

Madam Speaker, if I might quote one other comment, the Retail Council predicts, "a great wave of inflation will spread through the economy at this most damaging time imaginable." The Canadian Manufacturers' Association holds similar views. Its members are also very disturbed that officials of the minister's department are telling them to gear up for this change in legislation even before the legislation and its regulations are known in the final form.
Again, would the minister explain why he and his officials are trying to accelerate this process, because the diversion of management time and the diversion of the resources of companies will compound not just the inflation problem but the unemployment problem? There will be more lay-offs as a result of this.

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
subtopic: USE OF MANAGEMENT RESOURCES TO EFFECT CHANGE
speechtext: Madam Speaker, the hon. member has engaged in the same old game of raising fears and raising possibilities that are not in the offing whatsoever. The fact of the matter is that, in response to the representations that we received from the business community, we have delayed the implementation date so that it would be possible to have the fullest possible input from the business community. We are listening very carefully to their views. The subject matter has been studied for a great many years. As the hon. member knows, one of the basic and important purposes of this change is to put Canadian manufacturers in a position as equally favourable as those imported goods with which they must compete.

Since this shift is directly caused by government action, and because the government is so concerned about the impact of government actions on the inflationary process, would the minister agree at this time to defer the implementation of the shift in the sales tax indefinitely? Would he authorize hearings in the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs to hear these organizations which are so concerned about the inflationary impact, so that we can get to the bottom of the problem?

NATIONAL HARBOURS BOARD
subsubtopic: VANCOUVER WATER LOT LEASE INCREASES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Transport. The minister will know, as a result of a letter I sent to him on June 9, that some of the 1982 National Harbours Board water lot leases in the port of Vancouver have increased by close to 100 per cent. Many of the commercial and recreational leaseholders are facing increases this year of a substantial amount. This substantial increase, plus the increase of municipal property assessments in Vancouver's lower mainland, is threatening the financial viability of independent businessmen in the port of Vancouver. Some may be forced out of business.
In view of the disastrous effects these increases will have on the financial solvency of leaseholders, and the government's June 28 objective of a 6 per cent world, can the minister give this House the assurance that these 1982 increases will now be reviewed and that any increases after June 28 will be a maximum of 6 per cent?

speechtext: Madam Speaker, 1 would like to direct my question to the Minister of Finance. Banks are paying 13.75 per cent interest to people who have savings accounts with them. At the same time they are charging 22.5 per cent to customers who want loans. That is a spread of 8.75 per cent, an all-time high spread. Would the minister discuss with the banks the very serious effects on individuals, on farmers and on small-business men, which these exorbitant interest rates are causing, and urge the banks to reduce these high interest rates on loans, which will make the minister's objective of a 6 per cent inflation rate in the next year impossible?

EFFECT OF PROPOSED PRICE INCREASES ON INFLATION
speechtext: Madam Speaker, my supplementary is also directed to the Minister of Finance. Yesterday the Treasury Board secretary or chairman announced that the government intends to hang tough on rate increases for government-regulated industries but will not attempt to alter any oil pricing agreements to bring them in line with this wonderful and mythical world of 6 per cent. Statistics Canada today released its latest consumer price figures which show that commodities with high energy components, such as food products, continue to lead the way up the inflationary spiral. 1 wonder if I can have the attention of the Minister of Finance. He probably missed my preamble. I will do it again.

subtopic: EFFECT OF PROPOSED PRICE INCREASES ON INFLATION
speechtext: No, no.

subtopic: EFFECT OF PROPOSED PRICE INCREASES ON INFLATION
speechtext: Only the question matters.

subtopic: EFFECT OF PROPOSED PRICE INCREASES ON INFLATION
speechtext: How does the Minister of Finance think that the wonderful world of 6 per cent can be achieved if such an important cost component as energy, petroleum if you like, in food, transportation and home heating, will jump 10 per cent in September and 30 per cent next year? speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
subtopic: EFFECT OF PROPOSED PRICE INCREASES ON INFLATION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the hon. member should reflect a little bit on his question and understand that there are countries in the world which have totally absorbed the international price of energy and are running inflation rates presently much lower than in Canada. Therefore, to single out that component as a determinant of the inflation rate is going much too far. I can give the example of West Germany which, according to the OECD, will have an inflation rate next year of 3 per cent. They have already absorbed

the total international energy price. We have not yet absorbed that. We still have, and will continue to have, prices lower than the international price. Surely with that rate of entry for energy price increases into the economy, it should be possible for us to achieve a 6 per cent world next year that will provide the basis for recovery in the country.

speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce. What portion of the whole company will he get? Will it be a significant portion for that kind of money? Finally, why would he do it at all, given the economy of Canada today?

Coast Guard helicopters are generally not large enough to provide a primary search and rescue capability and consequently, specialized equipment such as rescue hoists, survival packages, life rafts and extensive radio communication equipment cannot be carried on board for that purpose.
6.	The Department of National Defence is charged with the responsibility for providing primary air resources in support of marine search and rescue. On the west coast this responsibility is discharged by 442 Squadron based at Comox on the east coast of Vancouver Island, whose resources consist of three Buffalo fixed-wing search aircraft and four Labrador/Voya-geur rescue helicopters. The helicopters carry five crew members, two of which are qualified search and rescue specialists.
Because the Department of Transport's responsibility is to provide marine resources for search and rescue, as opposed to air resources, and because Coast Guard helicopters are not capable of carrying out primary search and rescue operations, helicopter crews do not receive any formal training in search and rescue.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1982-83 MEASURE TO ESTABLISH

speechtext: The House resumed from Tuesday, July 20, 1982, consideration of the motion of Mr. Bussieres that Bill C-125, to provide supplementary borrowing authority, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs, and the amendment of Mr. Clark (p. 19456).

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1982-83 MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last evening I was discussing the fact that those on the opposite side of the House are noticeably quiet when it comes to condemning publicly the financial policies of the government. At that time I provided a long and detailed list of the many instances when shocking and wasteful spending on the part of this government and its agencies has resulted in taxpayers' dollars literally being thrown away. I mentioned how rare it was for anyone on the other side to object to the burden this was placing on all Canadians. The silence from the other side of the House has been deafening.
I mentioned, in particular, the Liberals' closed-mouth approach in their delay to call three byelections in Timiskam-ing, Broadview-Greenwood and Leeds-Grenville so that Canadians in those three ridings could have a voice in the House. I suggested that everyone, including those on the opposite side, knew that members of the government could not even bear to think of the humiliation they would receive at the polls if those byelections were called. Better to let thousands and thousands of Canadians remain unrepresented than to
July 21, 1982

embarrass the 145 opposite. If the thought of defeat in only three ridings is enough to cause those opposite to shudder, small wonder the government is absolutely refusing even to consider calling a general election. They certainly do not want to let voters in every riding have the opportunity to defeat the entire bunch, which is what would happen if Canadians were given the chance.
People across the nation know that the only 6 per cent solution to save this country is the one which results in the government being reduced to 6 per cent or less representation in Parliament. The government is asking Canadians to help it solve our problems. I can assure the House that they are trying to. Many Members of Parliament on all sides of the House, but especially those of us on this side of the House, are receiving letters, telephone calls and representations as to how we on this side, or Canadians in general, can get rid of the government. There is talk of petitions being presented across the country, in Liberal ridings as well. There are letters to the editors as to how the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) can be impeached. These letters come from people who consider that there is legislation in Canada similar to that in the United States where a president under certain circumstances can be impeached. Canadians would love to do something to change the government. They know that the government is the problem and only an election will provide us with a solution. Yet the government, clinging to power for the sake of power, has other ideas. It denies any and all responsibility. According to the government, the guilty culprits are Canadians.
The government says that Canadians expect too much. I suggest to those on the opposite side of the House that since Canadians are footing the bill and paying the shot, they have a right to their expectations. Canadians have a right to expect that the billions of dollars they pay in taxes each year will be spent wisely in their behalf.
Recently the Fraser Institute reported that the tax bill of the average Canadian family has increased by 619 per cent between 1961 and 1980. We can imagine how much it has increased and will increase by the end of 1982. The government simply legislates increases to its coffers, adding greed to arrogance and the quest to remain in power. Canadians have the right to expect that this extra money taken from them is being spent wisely in their behalf.
How wisely was it spent and in whose behalf when Petro-Canada gave $480,000 to 16 Norwegian and French oil drillers not to work? Each of these drillers was given $30,000 and sent home because officials at Petro-Canada neglected to read the relevant immigration regulation, or were totally unaware of its existence, the regulation which bars foreign workers from the jobs involved.
How wise was it when the CBC flew 74 people to Versailles to cover the summit conference when the Global and CTV networks sent over four people each? If the two privately-owned networks could provide excellent coverage of the event with four people each, why in heaven's name were 70 extra
Supplementary Borrowing Authority
people needed by the CBC? The trip to Versailles contained other vivid illustrations of the problems the government is causing.
Prior to Versailles the Prime Minister promised that he would return home with solutions to the economic morass his government had created in the country. He did not admit that his government had created the problems, just the opposite. He said that Canada's economic woes were the direct result of the policies of other nations, most notably the United States, so he would go to Versailles and tell the leaders of the other nations just how things should be done. As we all know, things did not quite work out that way. The leaders of the other nations were far too busy working out their own plans for economic growth to be bothered listening to the whines and complaints of a finger-pointer, so the Prime Minister returned home petulant and emptyhanded. Rather than making the trip to Versailles, the Prime Minister would have been well advised to travel along the road to Damascus.
A conversion is clearly in order. The Prime Minister must be converted from his thinking that the problems he has created are the fault of others. He must be converted from thinking that only he knows best what shape and form the nation should assume, and that the opposite opinions of others are to be dismissed out of hand. He must be converted from thinking that the power of his office is absolute and that he is not accountable to the people. He must be converted from thinking that the plight of the people is their own fault, and he must realize that it is the fault of his government. If the Prime Minister does not walk along the road to Damascus, the nation will continue on the road to ruin.
There is little hope the government will abandon its irresponsible spending. Right now it is before the House asking for authority to borrow $11 billion more. The Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) and the government should give this matter second thoughts. They know that when it is totalled it is more than they require. If they reduced this amount to $7 billion, it would probably be more in line with their actual needs. There is little hope the government will try to do much along this line or try to reduce the massive debt.
I feel very strongly that we in the House should not and must not approve this supplementary borrowing authority in its full amount. I would never approve throwing good money after bad, especially good money in the direction of a bad government. The hole in which the government has put the country is too massive and too costly to be overlooked. We may not be able to stop passage of the bill, but come the next election, Canadians will dig another hole and bury the government in it.
Columnists across the country have been writing scathing articles on the performance of the government. One appeared in the Tuesday, July 20 edition of The Toronto Sun entitled, "6 Per Cent Snake Oil". It contains many truths. In part it reads:
That beehive of mediocrity, the CBC, cost us $792.2 million this past year, a 10 per cent increase over the previous year.

July 21, 1982
Supplementary Borrowing Authority
Also it talked about Petro-Canada and what has gone on in that corporation. I should like to refer to another quotation of this very astute columnist, Laura Sabia, which reads:
Multiculturalism, bilingualism and metrication cost us billions of dollars we couldn't afford, taxpayers money poured into a bottomless pit.
The Fraser Institute recently published a report on taxes by all three levels of government.
As 1 mentioned before, this report showed astronomical increases in the tax bill placed upon the shoulders of average Canadian families which can ill afford them. It continued:
While jobs are lost everywhere, the economy is in shambles, the government increases its bureaucracy by 8,000-
I could go on and on with horror stories. I hope hon. members on all sides of the House will see that the $11 billion is asking for far too much and that it should be reduced. If not, of course we will be voting against Bill C-125 which will almost give the government a blank cheque to spend and spend and spend.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakeroldname: Mr. Douglas Fisher (Parliamentary Secretary to the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1982-83 MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to have an opportunity to rise and comment on this legislation today. I might add that I am looking forward to hearing the hon. member for Lincoln (Mr. Mackasey) later this afternoon who will be reflecting upon this bill in more detail than I am about to do.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1982-83 MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext: You are filibustering the bill.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1982-83 MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext: At this point I intend simply to pass along a few reactions I have had from listening to some of my colleagues and friends from all sides during the course of this debate when they talked about the economy and the government's management of it. I would also like to discuss how members opposite would offer alternatives to the Canadian people.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1982-83 MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext: Why do we not vote on it then?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1982-83 MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
On Monday, I listened with great interest to the right hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) who, I believe, made some unwarranted personal attacks which were basically attempts to demean the performance of the government rather than present alternatives. We have listened to this hollow discussion of government policies for some time during this debate. We have not heard from the other side the alternatives to current policies.
I believe all Canadians would welcome-I certainly would- the very refreshing insights into wasteful expenditures or expenditures which have not been agreed to. I believe that all Canadians would agree with any member who would rise in his place to suggest that an expenditure on one item would have been put to better use if it had been given to an ordinary person in need. I welcome those concerns.
I have listened to concerned members opposite talk about unemployment. For example, I believe that the hon. member for Athabasca (Mr. Shields) has given us a lucid and sincere description of unemployment in his riding. He has often
brought home to us the meaning of the slowdown in his riding owing to the energy policy. At the time it is not enough to raise small issues such as that of the brief cases and claim that unemployment in Athabasca will be solved by that issue. Instead, we on this side of the House are attempting to emphasize exactly what the hon. member for Athabasca has reminded us of, that government spending must go to people. I urge hon. members opposite to focus on government spending on services when they begin to present their alternatives.
I recall the debate on federal-provincial spending which took place in the House a few months ago. At that time we were discussing some $105 billion that the government is giving to the provinces in the form of transfer payments over the next five years. That money, which is gathered from Canadians all across the country, is being used to redistribute our resources to those people in need. Those expenditures are being used for universities, health care, and medicare. I felt that we had an excellent debate in the House because it focused on the qualities of those services and on the need for additional spending in those areas.
My hon. friend, the hon. member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn), whom I see across the way, while very often chastising us for our spending, shone in that debate because he was constantly urging that we spend more money for services rather than blindly cut back. It was that reasoned compassion that made his speeches so enlightening at that time. That same compassion expressed by the hon. member for Athabasca has often made his speeches compelling to those of us listening to them. That compassion and dedication which was so prevalent during that debate has made the Conservative speeches during this debate so hollow in its absence.
In this debate I would like to focus on some of the issues that are involved in our spending. With respect to unemployment, there are many members here who represent constituencies where unemployment is tragically high. Fortunately, unemployment levels are quite low in my riding and I, as well as the people in my riding, welcome the opportunity to share our strength and wealth with Canadians who are in greater need. This morning, I spoke on a radio talk show in Regina where numerous callers made the same point. The point they made was that the people in Regina, where unemployment is severe but not as great as in other parts of Canada, were prepared to share their wealth with those places which are in greater need. That is the purpose of our spending in Ottawa. Our role is to help Canadians overcome tragic economic periods like this and to benefit from our common prosperity. That sense of sharing is the motivation behind the spending which we have undertaken in so many of our programs.
I would refer hon. members to the speech of the right hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark). He had very little time for that type of concern in his speech. Instead, he spent most of his time delivering attacks, hollow rhetoric and vague discussions of government waste while throwing in one or two examples about taxis and briefcases, issues which he thought
July 21, 1982

significant. He did not tell us in any way how he would use this great nation's wealth to help those most in need.
He would not come to a riding such as mine where there is relative comfort and prosperity to tell my constituents how their great wealth could be used in less fortunate areas. It is hollow arguments such as these which I believe have cost the party opposite dearly.
I listened with equal interest to some of the speeches made by members of the New Democratic Party. I was disappointed, however, by those speeches because I often look to them to give us some motivation beyond the rhetoric which we hear in the House. I believe that those members usually remind us of the lives of ordinary Canadians. But we did not hear that during this debate. I challenge some of them to rise to the occasion and give us a decent speech dealing with how the government should use its resources in the future.
The speech of the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Fulton) was a grand old piece of rhetoric about the sins of capitalism, and the two old line parties which he called Tweedle-dum and Tweedle-dee. We heard this rhetoric years ago and it has been worn out and tired for decades.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1982-83 MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext: It is still true.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1982-83 MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
The hon. member says that it is still true. It is not true. It has not stood the test of history. What has stood the test of history in his party has been an open concern for the ordinary Canadian. His party has often presented that concern very well but they have failed in this debate.
Why am I constantly coming back to this question? Why am 1 suggesting a discussion that we have a discussion about the people instead of a debate on hollow rhetoric?

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1982-83 MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext: To waste time.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1982-83 MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext: I am doing it because the deficit today is a result of the government's expenditures on people and its response to a severe recession. This is not a hollow issue. This deficit is not to serve new programs, new expenditures or untried ideas. It is rather, a result of an attempt to solve difficulties and suffering caused by the recession. I suggest it would be a betrayal of our fellow Canadians to ignore that suffering by resorting to hollow political rhetoric-

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1982-83 MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext: Is that why you introduced closure?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1982-83 MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
-which we heard from the Leader of the Conservative Party and the first speaker from the New Democratic Party. We have a very severe problem which is clearly typified by the size of the government's deficit and our borrowing requirements.
We on this side take that very, very seriously. The minister has indicated that his budget has been brought down in response to the recession. He has indicated that the new demands caused by the severity, the depth and the speed of the recession were his motivation in preparing his June budget. In that budget he has given us an answer to the human problems
Supplementary Borrowing Authority
and the suffering reflected in the recession, answers that did not come forward from either the Official Opposition or its leader, or from the New Democratic Party. I refer specifically to the 6 per cent world that the government is proposing to all Canadians. The 6 per cent world is a manageable target which will bring all of us personal relief from the great ravages of inflation and the great demands and pressures of our recession. The 6 per cent world is our strength. The 12 per cent world is a continued world of weakness. I look forward to the time when the Conservative Party will be able to react to people instead of advancing hollow rhetoric, when it will be able to react to the specific problems of the economy rather than play phony games in this House. I think our fellow Canadians are asking us for that kind of sincerity and reflection on all sides.
When we hear about the 6 per cent world as presented in the budget, we are also hearing about the minister's great concern for the debt burden being carried by the government. We do not want to add to that at all. When we look we can see a marvellous compromise between the demands of the economy today, the great needs of ordinary people, and the need for prudent government.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1982-83 MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext: Is that why you increased the rent in Banff?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1982-83 MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext: We see aid for housing going out to the tune of $400 million, aid to small businesses amounting to another $400 million, several hundred millions of dollars for job creation and $100 million for the Farm Credit Corporation. All this money is being aimed at Canadians in great need.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1982-83 MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext: Raising taxes.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1982-83 MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext: It is not being aimed at wasteful ideas or new, untried schemes, it is certainly stemming from a much greater consciousness and awareness of the economy and of the people than was reflected by the Leader of the Opposition the other day. Hundreds of millions of dollars are being sent to people in great need, all coming as a result of our ability to find those savings inside our budget, to reorder our priorities and to put that money into much more needy areas, taking it from areas where there can be genuine savings without creating suffering. That is a response to the great problems that our economy faces and it has been reflected, since the budget, in much more hopeful attitudes among the Canadian people. We can look through sector after sector, area after area, towns and cities across this country, where people have said that the budget is offering them hope to get out of our current trouble.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1982-83 MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext: Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1982-83 MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
For example, the budget has been very well received in the housing sector. The housing sector has seen the hundreds of millions of dollars that we are offering this year alone, and they also see the great hope contained in the new tax proposals currently under study. Those proposals will bring permanent relief to that industry. That industry has responded from coast to coast by telling us that we have indeed given it the help it wants in order to build the homes needed by young

July 21, 1982
Supplementary Borrowing Authority
Canadians. That is money that we found in response to specific human problems, and money that we found without adding a new burden to the deficit. That is a reasonable response to a great problem and an alternative that we unfortunately did not hear from the hon. member speaking for the New Democratic Party when he talked about tweedledum and tweedledee or the ills of capitalism or whatever other hollow argument he put forward for 40 minutes, which had nothing to do with the way ordinary Canadians live.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1982-83 MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext: Not true.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1982-83 MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext: That hollow approach was very sadly put forward by our good friends in the New Democratic Party whose ideas we usually deeply respect, and an equally hollow approach was put forward by a man held in great esteem by his fellow Canadians, the Leader of the Opposition. Those hollow arguments are great failures in the middle of a debate and an emergency like this. Let our fellow Canadians know that sly phrases about briefcases, or silly little references to funny money, or some kind of personal attack against the minister are not answers to serious economic issues. The American deficit is clearly related to military spending. The concern in the business community in the United States is what will happen when their economy recovers. What proportion of their GNP will be directed to reducing their deficit, or will it continue to be the policy in the United States to carry on massive spending on the military? That is the real problem bothering the Americans. It is a legitimate concern. It is probably the greatest defender of democracy in the world, but the role they have to play today as opposed to the eastern bloc, the role Great Britain used to play, is the need to arm, to spend on the military, to be vigilant. What makes the business community in the United States apprehensive about their deficit is that they perpetually ask themselves, "If we borrow to spend and borrow for this reason or that reason, how do we know that our government, the American government, will work assiduously to bring down the deficit, which is costly, which theoretically competes with private enterprise for the pool of capital, which is not all that large?"
Our deficit is entirely different. It reflects the nature of Canada. It reflects our conviction that the have provinces must help the have-not provinces. It reflects our commitment in the Constitution to the concept of transfer payments. It reflects the obligation of the central government to help the less fortunate, less wealthy provinces, through the system of transfers.
Then we have the massive unemployment problem in this country. There are automatic regulators built into our economic system. That increases the outflow of transfers to the provinces, if only to look after the outflow of welfare payments in those provinces as represented by the Canada Assistance Plan.
The other addition to our deficit, which is automatic, and thank God it is, is the payment of the unemployment insurance benefits to those less fortunate than ourselves who, for no reason of their own, are out of work and very dependent on unemployment insurance benefits. It is no mystery to anyone in the House of Commons that when you have 1.5 million people out of work, the cash flow problems of unemployment insurance are real and must be met by the government. They are reflected in the deficit.
By the same token, when the economy starts to recover in Canada, unlike the United States, when unemployment is reduced, employment begins to increase again and the numbers of unemployed start to decrease, immediately and automatically the transfers of money through the Canada Assistance Plan will be substantially less. The pay-outs under unemployment insurance will be substantially less. Automatically the deficit shrinks at an amazingly rapid rate. It is significant, when you look at the figures for 1978 and 1979, that our deficit in those days was about 5.2, as opposed to 5.4 today.

I do not think hon. members opposite will make many yards by preaching gloom and doom when they sense, finally, that there is leadership, the proper budget is in place, the deficit is under control, the dollar is strengthening, inflation is on its way down and, perhaps more importantly, the government's policy of restraint is being well accepted by the Canadian work force.
I took the trouble yesterday, along with hon. members from all parties, to sit in a committee. I have forgotten the name of the committee. After a while all committees look alike. It may have been the Standing Committee on Miscellaneous Estimates. However, there we met with articulate, intelligent union leaders representing, for the most part, members of the civil service. Another group was representing railway unions. The press was there. Some newer members of the House were apprehensive about the approach of the union leaders. What happened was that the unions representing railway workers and those speaking for public servants last night showed an appreciation that a 6 per cent-5 per cent policy would work; that if we all accept restraint, inflation will come down; and that for every 1 per cent drop in inflation there will be an equivalent 1 per cent increase in real wages. We are not running into any opposition from the labour movement, organized labour, the public service or railway workers toward those of us fortunate enough to have a full-time job and those of us who are paid wages from the taxes of the average Canadian citizen-as the hon.

member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Evans) reminded us a week or so ago. The unions are saying that they are quite prepared to accept the concept of restraint. Basically, Canadians from coast to coast are saying that they are prepared to show some restraint if that will bring down inflation and put an end to unemployment and let industry grow and assume its usual competitive place in the world.
Last night the union representatives said, in effect, that they are prepared to be part of the fight against inflation because they want to be competitive when the markets of this country's customers improve. When the United States economy improves they want to be competitive. They realize that Canada is not competitive when the rate of inflation is 12 per cent while that of other countries with raw materials is two, three or four per cent.
Canadians today are sophisticated. The average worker is a highly educated, well-read person who understands economics. He understands that inflation is devastating. He understands the impact of inflation on fixed incomes and its negative impact on jobs. He understands that somehow we have to bring it to an end, but what he wants from the government, and what he is getting, is leadership.

The point I am getting at is that the problems in Canada are not unique to Canada. It is only the opposition which tries to create the false impression that somehow this government has stumbled into an economic recession unique to Canada, when in fact the evidence is to the contrary. Mr. Speaker, I am very grateful to my hon. colleagues on both sides of the House for their enthusiastic reception this afternoon. It must be the first time since I became a member of the House that I have had such a warm welcome from the other side, and on this side I see my colleague from Charlesbourg (Mr. Bussieres), originally from Roberval or more exactly from Normandin-he also happens to have a cottage at Saint-Thomas Didyme-who is quite agreeable to my speaking this afternoon, and my colleague from Roberval (Mrs. Beauchamp-Niquet) who is probably delighted with the prospect that I might mention her riding as well.
This afternoon, the debate is on the bill to provide borrowing authority for the government, and I have listened to the criticism levelled by members on the other side of the House. They are saying that the government's deficit is horrendous and outrageous and that this country is going down the drain, but if we look at the budget speech by the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) it says to what extent the government's revenues have been cut, and that the recession, as mentioned on page 3 of the budget speech, has caused a serious worsening of the government's fiscal position, and that the sharp fall in federal revenues is the inevitable consequence of a decline in production, employment and income. According to the minister's speech, the revenue loss attributable to the recession is estimated to be about $4.5 billion in 1982-83.
If we compare what the budget speech tells us about the government's loss of revenue with what members opposite have been demanding, namely, that the government intervene in several economic activity sectors including agriculture, small-and medium-sized businesses and housing, we get the following picture. We have a worldwide economic recession, although many Canadians may prefer to forget this and seem to be
Supplementary Borrowing Authority
saying that it may be happening in the United States but here in Canada we are not being affected. Well, I think that since the June 28 budget was brought down, and with the figures submitted by the Minister of Finance, people can see for themselves what effect this worldwide recession is having on Canada. So, on the one, hand we have the recession and the government's loss of revenue, and on the other hand, we have popular pressure being brought to bear on the government to spend money on certain economic activity sectors, and Mr. Speaker, when it comes down to it, there is a lot of money involved, and during the debate on this bill, it is up to all members of this House, members from Quebec and Ontario and all the other provinces, it is up to all members on the government side to clarify the situation for the Canadian people.
In any case, it is agreed that there is an economic recession, and the Canadian economy is unfortunately being affected by U.S. and world events, but on the other hand, to meet the many requests for assistance from various industrial sectors, we must find the necessary financial resources and act responsibly as a government in helping those activity sectors that have been severely affected by the recession, and we must explain to the Canadian people that nevertheless, because of our wealth of resources and borrowing opportunities, we can and must borrow in order to help these activity sectors. That is why the Minister of Finance said on June 28 in his budget speech: The result is that the projected budgetary deficit is very much higher than that forecast in the November budget.
I do not think that it in any way diminishes the government to admit that the situation did not develop as it was expected to, and that unfortunately, it has deteriorated as a result of the world situation, and we therefore have to act responsibly as Canadians. So what do we do? Do we raise taxes, to have more funds in the government treasury or are we going to cut expenditures and then borrow money to show certain sectors that we are willing to help them? In this kind of situation, Mr. Speaker, the government had to make a choice and it did. During the next two years, by setting a ceiling on wage increases in the public sector and sectors directly related to it, including government agencies, the government intends to reduce wage increases in order to save so many million dollars, money which will then be available for job-creation programs, assistance to farmers and to small and medium-sized businesses. This is how the Canadian government, the Liberal Party now in power, has faced up to its responsibilities, and then we hear the members opposite saying that the deficit is outrageous and that something must be done to bring the deficit back to more reasonable levels. However, they do not tell us what they mean by a reasonable deficit. They do not tell us what are the serious alternatives. Of course, they will tell me that this is according to parliamentary practice. The

government is in place and the opposition criticizes, whether solutions exist or not. So when the government suggested after the budget that wage increases be capped at 6 and 5 per cent for the next two years, it planned to use this money and the amounts saved by reducing the expenditures of various agencies to give assistance to farmers.
When we look at page 25 of the budget papers and see the special programs developed to provide financial assistance for the farmers, either directly, or else indirectly if the members opposite prefer, we must realize that if these programs are to be funded, we must have the necessary tax revenues. That is how I analyse the situation when considering those programs, the housing programs and those intended for small businesses. But how can the borrowing power bill now before the House be important indirectly when it comes to funding the farm assistance program and the financial commitments of the various departments? We need money and that is what we were asked by the farmers, those of Quebec, for instance. If I remember what happened in my own constituency, it is probably because the same thing happened in several others. 1 see next to me my colleague, the hon. member for Lac St-Jean (Mr. Gimai'el) who also received representations as well as my colleague, the hon member for Roberval. My colleague, the hon. member for Temiscamingue (Mr. Tousignant) and my colleague, the hon. member for Kamouraska-Riviere-du-Loup (Mr. Gendron) also received representations from farmers. The Minister of State for Finance, the hon. member for Charlesbourg, does not have as many farmers in his constituency as I have in mine, in fact I do not think he has many, but in any case, we received many representations from farmers who told us: We need money because the international financial situation has brought about a recession that is affecting Canadian farmers, and they need money from the Canadian government under the loan programs of the Canadian Farm Credit Corporation. What was the answer of the Canadian government? This is what I find on page 25 of the budget papers:
Over the next two years loans totalling $200 million will be made under the program to farmers in financial distress. The loans will be made at the regular FCC interest rate (currently 16'/>
per cent) but a rebate of 4 percentage points will be provided for the first two years of the loan. The government is allocating $100 million to the program ($84 million as a special contribution to the FCC for lending to farmers and $16 million to pay for the interest rebates) and the FCC will divert $116 million to the program from its regular lending fund.
What is important is that this program came into force immediately. Moreover, the usual conditions offered by the corporation will still apply. For instance, the ceilings of $300,000 for individuals and $500,000 for associations will still apply, but the loans will not be restricted to the usual customers of the Farm Credit Corporation, namely young farmers, small operators and new farmers. Many people told us about the situation of farmers. Of course, there are farmers over 45 and 50 who have been in farming for many years and are in a
good financial position or at least have the financial backing to face the situation. However, the fact is that young farmers will be in difficulty if the Canadian government fails to develop programs and provide access to additional funds.
In response to those representations we have introduced a special farm financial assistance program. Another significant aspect is that the small business development program referred to on page 23 of the budget papers is available to farmers as well and there is no requirement that they be incorporated. That is indeed an important consideration for young farmers who want to invest or expand. As I said, if a young farmer is not financially as well off as his father or the people from whom he is buying the farm-or even with the case of people who have been in the business for only a few years-it can be readily understood that he is not quite prepared to come to grips with the situation created by the economic recession and high interest rates. That is why under the small business development program a farmer will also be eligible for interest rates 4 per cent below the prevailing rates. I think that is very important for our young farmers and for other young people who want to become farmers and who, in the present economic context, have certain obligations to meet. Another significant aspect is that we met with APU spokesmen who referred to the current situation and mentioned the funds earmarked for the agricultural sector in the November 1981 budget; they felt that the program was commendable but that perhaps more money ought to be made available. They were making representations, of course, and as a result we responded by introducing a special assistance program for farmers. I may be repeating myself, Mr. Speaker, but we cannot say that we are going to launch various assistance programs and then find out that the recession has been cutting into our revenues. That explains why we have to borrow, hence the bill we have before us.
I have just referred to something which farmers find very important, the question of the great number of small businesses in the riding of Lotbiniere, particularly in the Bois-Francs area and in the rest of the riding. I could mention the various ridings of members who are here today, particularly those of the province of Quebec who come from such regions as Montreal or Quebec City, Beauce, Bois-Francs and Sague-nay-Lac-Saint-Jean where there are many small- and mediumsized businesses. It has been said that Quebec is their paradise, which immediately brings to mind certain regions such as Beauce, Saguenay-Lac-Saint-Jean or Bois-Francs.

Temiscamingue as well. My colleague from Temiscamingue did not want me to forget his region which is also developing rapidly. I can tell the House that since the member for Temiscamingue (Mr. Tousignant) has been here in Ottawa, since his election in 1979, he has done a lot of work to promote the development of his region. Many representations were made to members on behalf of small businesses and
July 21, 1982

their spokesmen mentioned the small business bond which was first called the small business development bond, and they said that this program had been extremely useful to small business until December 1981. After the November budget it was called the small business bond and at the time people were talking about businesses in financial difficulties. When they heard about those two programs, a great many people said to us: Listen, as in any other sector of economic activity, now that we have this program concerning the small business development bond and the small business bond, the banks will have to lower their rates.
In view of the fact that some banks had to limit their granting of credit unfortunately they were unable to accept the applications filed by a number of people in connection with that program. This explains why we received representations to the effect that although the program was satisfactory its mechanism was defective. Then the Minister of State for Small Businesses and Tourism (Mr. Lapointe) came up with some suggestions which have been passed on to him by the member for Temiscamingue the member for Kamouraska-Riviere-du-Loup, the member for Roberval, the member for Lac-Saint-Jean and other members on this side of the House. In their view the program was adequate, the people found it satisfactory, but its mechanism in dealing with our banking institutions was faulty. Without passing judgement on those institutions, we are told that such a mechanism should be improved to provide greater flexibility. Then we can see on page 23 of the budget papers tabled on the evening of June 28, that the federal government is allocating $400 million in order to reduce interest costs by up to 4 percentage points for two years on borrowing by small businesses to finance new investment and research and development. Today, this makes a difference ... I can see that the Minister of State for Finance is leaving but he will surely be back to congratulate me at the end of my speech. Businesses now applying to financial institutions will be in a position to borrow at the rate set by the bank and afterwards, whatever their financial circumstances as far as the Department of Revenue is concerned, the Canadian government will directly reimburse 4 per cent to the bank. That makes a considerable difference which is why we needed $400 million to provide some financial assistance to farmers. It does not necessarily mean that as a result of all those programs implemented under the budget, the Canadian government needed the borrowing power requested in Bill C-125 before us but part of those funds were necessary to improve Canada's financial position and to maintain its competitiveness on foreign markets; in the case of my own province this level has decreased. Very few comments were made about the Quebec government, but while we are told that we should promote our Canadian and Quebec tourist industry, the Quebec Premier is not showing leadership in this field since he chose to go to the United States. Anyway, funds had to be allocated to that
Supplementary Borrowing Authority
program in response to the demand expressed throughout Canadan and mainly in my province. Some financial assistance was requested for small businesses.
The reaction mentioned by my colleague Louis Duclos in his speech was this: should we at this time in answer to the expectations of our businesses increase taxes? Are the present economic conditions normal and can we increase taxes or should we instead divert funds obtained by reducing government expenditures and with our borrowing power provide financial assistance to businesses and to farmers?
As I was saying, before digressing on the province of Quebec and the leader of its government, the Premier of Quebec, those are things people have been clamouring for. To my mind, as a responsible government it was our duty to help major industries in every one of the provinces whichever they may be; some provinces do have economic activities that are more important than others. We just had to respond to the expectations of Canadians in that regard. Since the budget was brought down on June 28th, many of our constituents have told us: We heard the Minister of Finance and the comments of journalists; we have examined the main thrust of your budget; we think it's okay. How is it, then, that there has been so much carping, at least during the first few days following its tabling; how come, when it only aims at helping the industries that have asked for assistance?
Little by little, Mr. Speaker-and I see my colleague from Charlesbourg smile with delight-it is true, many people are beginning to comment favourably on the budget, on its impact, on the meetings between the Right Hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and representatives of industry, business and labour and on the rate of inflation being reduced to 6 and 5 per cent. Of course, there may be some groups who feel uneasy about the 6 per cent ceiling or reduction in private enterprise, and I mean the unions. But as the latest polls have demonstrated that 80 per cent of workers would rather accept a cut in salary than lose their jobs, I feel that the introduction of our budget and public awareness of the situation only confirm the soundness of the Minister of Finance's decision to reduce expenses through the 6 and 5 per cent caps, not to increase taxes and to borrow wherever we can so that we may respond to the expectations of Canadians.
We now hear more and more people say: Listen: let governments set the example, starting with MPs. Well, Mr. Speaker, that has now been done. From this month onwards-although we have not heard much about it in the media-all Members of Parliament, on both sides of the House, senators and ministers, will accept a cut in salary. There has been much ado about the civil servants and things like that, but we were the first ones to admit that we feel we have decent salaries and are willing to take a cut to prove to Quebecers and other Canadians that we, too, want to do our part to aid our ailing Canadian economy, that we want that money invested in various

July 21, 1982
Supplementary Borrowing Authority
programs; and tell the civil service: look, we took a cut ourselves. This has not been made known sufficiently, I think. That is why 1 wanted to emphasize this point this afternoon, and remind people that we always practise what we preach.
In this instance, MPs have paved the way, extending it right across the public service. As a result, people come to us and say: We agree with the 6 per cent ceiling and objective. Several days ago, I read articles saying the strategy would not work, that is was not serious. Then, suddenly, a few days later, we see the opposite. The Canadian government wants to reduce expenditures and, through the bill which is now before the House, channel those funds toward sectors of the economy that need them most.
One industry has always been a major one throughout Canada, and especially in my own province, namely the housing industry. In Quebec, people tend to say that if the construction industry is okay, everything is okay. I could mention again a number of ridings and areas where this is especially true, but I know their members are here in the House to discuss various problems, so let us say that the expression is a popular one throughout the province. This particular sector needs financial help and there have been a number of meetings and representations and conversations with various members on the subject.
I remember a few months ago when we discussed the mortgage renewal program, people said we did not go far enough. This time, we have gone further, Mr. Speaker, but now they are complaining that the deficit is too high and we should not have gone about it in this way. Well, if that is not a double standard, what is? Either we help the sectors that are asking for help or we do not help them, and considering the drop in government revenues, what are we supposed to do? We have to borrow. So I mean, it is no use shilly-shallying. This is a time for action, and that is why I wish the members opposite would realize what they are saying. They want us to help certain industrial sectors and then, they wonder, when the recession causes a sharp drop in government revenues, why we want to introduce a borrowing authority bill. Mr. Speaker, I say they should wake up. It is as plain as the nose on anyone's face what the government's choice must be. I think the situation is such that money must be injected into the housing industry and we must help first-time home buyers.
Mr. Speaker, I have received any number of telephone calls from contractors and real estate agents asking about the program, who wanted me to send them some literature to explain how the program works, and I am doing just that, Mr. Speaker. In addition, housing co-operatives and rental housing will also benefit from the budget measures. Here we have an economic sector that is of major importance to Canada and to my province, and in the present situation, the Canadian
government has decided to provide incentives for home builders to start building by a certain date and for Canadians to buy their first home, either a new home or an existing one-in the case of an existing home, the $3000 grant also applies, provided the person is a first-time home buyer. Just think how many jobs will be generated! 1 was told that those programs may provide homes for 100,000 prospective home owners across Canada. Well, Mr. Speaker, it is probably true that when the construction industry is okay, everything is okay.
These incentives are still extremely beneficial to the economy of Quebec, Canada, Ontario, and all the provinces. Of course, the members opposite have not dwelt on those $3,000 and that program developed by the government. They talk about the deficit and tell us: "Of course, those things are important." Another program was also developed, and 1 see that my colleague for Charlesbourg, the Minister of State for Finance is smiling because he knows how hard he and his colleague, the Minister of Finance, had to work on those various programs to help Canadians face the present situation. For the Residential Rehabilitation Assistance Program, the amount of $30 million was mentioned at one time. Everyone of us received information on that program, which is the counterpart of the rural program underwhich many residents of rural municipalities in Canada, and especially in Quebec, since 1 am speaking about my own province, were eligible for assistance in the form of a $3,750 grant and loans of up to $10,000. Many people in Quebec, in my constituency, were asking: "Why is it that people in rural areas can benefit from this program and we cannot if our municipality has a population of over 2,500?" Mr. Speaker, the Residential Rehabilitation Assistance Program, under which $30 million were allocated originally, was developed to meet these expectations of Quebecers and Canadians, and following certain representations, the funding was increased to $60 million. While we are providing incentives, the members opposite and many people who do not agree with our political philosophy tell us that what we need are incentives.
Money has to be allocated to various programs so that the economy may grow in spite of the economic problems, in spite of the recession. But what are we to do? Once again, are we to increase taxes or, if we have to inject some money into the economy in spite of our deficit, should we still fund such programs? I say yes, Mr. Speaker, and that is what we did on June 28. I can hear a member of the New Democratic Party say: "Sure!" He therefore agrees with me. Even though we are injecting money into the economy, we must still be able to say to the Canadian people: "We are not increasing your taxes, but due to the economic situation, we are taking action to urge the Canadian people to work, and housing is an extremely important sector."
Mr. Speaker, another program that is important for many members of Parliament and many Quebecers and Canadians is the job-creation program, particularly the Community
July 21, 1982

Development Program and various other related programs. In many, if not all ridings, many people took part in what used to be called the Canada Works Program, now the Community Development Program. They have gained experience, they have done very significant things for the economy of their ridings or their regions and were able to obtain grants because of the unemployment rate in their community. I could repeat the names of all the constituencies and all the hon. members who have benefited from various programs, but I shall name only one, Roberval, with which I am somewhat familiar. In the Lac Saint-Jean region, we have the Dolbeau Western Village which many people from Quebec and the rest of Canada visit each year during the western festival.
Huge sums of money were allocated for a community development program and we were able to provide jobs for the people of Dolbeau. As my colleague said, 40 jobs were created and money was earmarked for promoting the tourist industry in that riding, more precisely in Dolbeau, and it is through Canada Works projects that construction and infrastructures were made possible in the Western Village of Dolbeau and in other cases that involved summer employment. So that was money well spent, rightfully spent and, by dint of reviewing and reshaping that type of program and the administrative regulations, a great number of people are able to get things done. Granted, one could say those jobs last a limited period of time, but our attitude is certainly different from that of our colleagues opposite who tried to govern-I say "tried"-and seeked to put an end to those programs.

Mr. Speaker, in closing, I would like to say in view of those jobs creating and economy-boosting programs, when we consider the representations that were made and the fact that people now talk openly about the budget, that the Canadian government has carried out its responsibilities without raising taxes. Funds were allocated to programs designed to assist Canadians despite a worldwide recession, and economic hardships that affect every country in the world including our own. If we are asked today to give the government the borrowing authority they request it is to allow Canadians to live in this country and support their families. It was the responsibility of the Canadian government to introduce a budget and to allocate funds to various programs and that is why we directly need this borrowing authority and that is why, Mr. Speaker, I will support the bill.

Mr. Speaker, I doubt very much that it will do any good to try to calm down the rabbling hordes on the other side and I appreciate your attempt to do so.
I would like to discuss this matter and try to clarify some of the issues and points which have been raised by hon. members opposite with regard to the borrowing authority bill, how it relates to the over-all economic policy of the government and what has caused the need for this increase in borrowing authority. I would like to discuss the deficit in the context of showing that, in fact, the increase in the deficit that we have seen is substantially and structurally different from the deficit being faced, for example, in the United States. I would like to discuss my belief that the Canadian financial system can indeed support the kind of deficit which was forecast in the financial statements of the government as of June 28. 1 would like to discuss some of the recent activities and words of the opposition with regard to their ideas as to how the deficit might be dealt with. It has been saying that it is a terrible deficit and that initial programs of restraint should be brought in immediately. The opposition has put forward ideas of how restraint could be applied to resolve our problems, such as the suggestion not to buy briefcases.
The President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Johnston) has clearly indicated that we on this side of the Elouse will certainly support the members of the oppostion if they can show that there is waste in any area of government. If that can be shown, we on this side of the House will certainly do everything in our power to eradicate that waste from government. It is easy to pick up areas of spending which can be blown out of proportion and put in such a context that it appears that there is waste. But when one looks down underneath the surface of the problem and considers the actual expenditure, more times than not-and the Auditor General's report will back me up time and time again-

Let us take the example cited by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) the other day. He suggested that it would resolve our deficit problem if brief cases were not purchased by the government for use by public servants. We are talking about a deficit that is substantial; there can be no doubt about

that. That deficit has to be reduced in an orderly way that will not trip the heart out of the Canadian economy or the Canadian social system.
Let us look at the question. When I was in the public service working with the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, a great many demands were placed on public servants to travel about this country and to interact with provincial counterparts and the business community. Day after day members opposite demand that we consult with the business community, other levels of government, private interest groups and individual Canadians. They demand that we get the message of what the federal government is all about to Canadians. In that process, public servants travel.
1 am not going to stand here and say there are not occasions, just as there are in private business, where there may be an abuse of travel requirements. Long before this issue was raised by the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Fulton), the President of the Treasury Board commissioned a report into travel. That report should be available shortly. We will then see how much substance there is with regard to the question of government travel.
If the NDP feels we should cut out travel by public servants, eliminate all of it, that would effectively shut down the federal government. We could forget about consulting business communities in various corners of the country, forget about making the federal presence felt in various corners of this country and forget about consulting with provincial governments. If there is waste, we will eradicate that, but 1 do not have any delusions that there will be a vast reduction in travel because of waste. There may be a reduction of travel-

The hon. member is wrong. He should listen to the members of his own party. The hon. member for Skeena was talking about travel inside the country and travel outside the country. He was talking about travel by public servants both inside and outside Canada.
I am telling the hon. member that if there is an abuse of travelling being done by public servants, it will be eradicated. I predict the report will confirm that there is very little abuse with regard to travel. In the federal system such as we have with the opposition demanding day after day that we not introduce policies without consulting, the requirement of travel is very real.
There very well could be introduced a restraint program where the government will only permit one half the travelling, that it will only pay the cost of that number. However, there would be more difficulty in communicating and formulating policy at the federal level. That will be a fact of life that has to

be considered. That is what the report of the President of the Treasury Board will indicate. If there is a need for restraint, we will thank hon. members for having brought it to our attention, although it had already received the attention of the President of the Treasury Board who commissioned a study into it long before it was raised by the hon. member for Skeena.
We hear condemnations of the public service. The official opposition is schizophrenic on this issue. From time to time it stands up as the defender of the Public Service of Canada, stating that the government is a harsh employer, that it is terrible and the opposition would be much better. Let us look at the facts.
We hear the Leader of the Opposition talk about the public service squandering money all over the place. Let us look back to the last election and, in fact, the 1979 election. There have been two interruptions by members on the other side. I appreciate the fact that our beloved House leader has jumped into the fray to help straighten these things out. More times than not, Mr. Speaker, as you are aware having sat in the chair, we have been ready to vote on many things and other members have not showed up. As a matter of fact, they took 16 days off just a little while ago. But that is water under the bridge.
With regard to the borrowing authority, the Government of Canada, in order to carry out the various programs it has in place, needs this borrowing requirement. Members on the other side say that we should be cutting government waste. Yet when we ask where we should be making these cuts, they fly off in all different directions. There are those who say that we could cut government waste by doing away with the famous brief cases. That matter was brought up by the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark). We heard that this would save perhaps $400,000, that it is a lot of money for most people in Canada. I would not call the hon. leader Mr. Joe Briefcase. I reject that being said by anyone in this House. He
is not Mr. Joe Briefcase. He is the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition and I ask all members here to respect that fact, because it is important.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

I hear the hon. member on the other side saying be gentle. I will be gentle with hon. members. The hon. member is just back from Strasbourg. I welcome him back in the House; we missed him very much. We should be gentle with one another in this House. We should indeed be gentle with our civil servants.
Many people have said that civil servants are the ones who will be carrying all of the burden for the people of Canada by having their increases reduced to 6 per cent and 5 per cent.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext: You are speaking on Bill C-124 again.

I am bringing this in along with the borrowing bill. We know that the civil servants, by and large, are very strong contributors to the strength of this country. It would be wrong for them solely to bear this burden of taking 6 per cent in one year and 5 per cent in another unless we asked this of all the people of Canada. I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that if all of the people of Canada do get together and restrain themselves-and I am talking here about Members of Parliament and the Government of Canada-then I am sure we can face this problem that is now weighing so heavily on all of our shoulders. I am sure we can get the solutions that we are going to need.
The hon. member for Ottawa Centre who spoke just before me talked about newsprint. Newsprint is of great importance in my riding because we have four paper mills there. I am happy to say that one of the paper mills, Ontario Paper, received a grant from the federal government of $12 million to help it renew its newsprint factory to make it more competitive.

In my opinion, this is the right direction because it helps to protect our jobs. It helps us in those areas which need help the most.
I would like to address myself to what the Minister of State for International Trade (Mr. Lumley) said today. In the Niagara peninsula, we have many automotive workers; some 8,000 of them work for General Motors and related industries. Today, the decision to let up a little on Japanese cars coming into the country was one which possibly will be well taken by people in other parts of the country. But I can tell hon. members that for us it will mean more hardship until we do have these content rules put in. I would urge hon. members in this House to stick together and see if we can get the answers to lead us out of the morass that we seem to be in. This applies not only to Canada but to many of the western industrialized countries of the world. It will not be done by heckling one another-

It is most important for us as members of Parliament to listen to what each of us has to say, and as one of my colleagues noted, it must also be realized that all the problems cannot be solved by a single group of Canadians, namely public servants.

I believe it is incumbent upon all of us to carry the burden as much as we can. These were the few comments I wanted to interject into this debate. As hon. members were saying earlier, we are always amenable to discussions and to a happy resolution of the problems. We look forward to the vote whenever it comes.

Mr. Speaker, it gives me pleasure to take part in this debate on Bill C-125 and the amendment moved by the Right Hon. Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Clark) to reduce the government's borrowing power. I am going to deal particularly with the amendment because it is the crux of the present debate. In my view, this is just an exercise in futility because it will get us nowhere, and is only a scheme to thwart the financial and borrowing plans of the government, and make this House of Commons lose more time in the fall. In fact, Bill C-125 does not allocate funds or decide whether or not a certain amount can be spent on such and such a program. It only empowers the government to borrow $11 billion. Government expenditure will be studied through the appropriation bill, first in Parliament and then in the Standing Committee that will report to the House for the final vote. So, if the House of Commons does not agree with government expenditures it will not appropriate them. The claim that Bill C-125 will result in huge government expenditures and the attempt to lead us into a debate on government spending, may be politically wise but I think it is important to emphasize that this bill does not appropriate funds. The appropriation of funds is a different process and this bill only gives the government the authority to borrow to cover its deficit. Now, why is the deficit higher or why do we expect it to be higher in the present fiscal year than was expected in November? The answer is simple. Early last winter, depression set in all over the world, particularly the United States and that put pressures on the federal budget in two ways. First, federal revenues decreased significantly. The June 28th budget
Supplementary Borrowing Authority
forecast a reduction of about $6.4 billion. That is because companies and businesses will be making less profit, but also because there will be a lot more unemployed people who will earn less money and, therefore, will pay less income tax.
The second pressure brought to bear on the budget of the federal government has to do with the fact that over the years we have introduced in our system what we call stabilizers, social programs such as unemployment insurance and the Canada Assistance Plan which pays for 50 per cent of ail social assistance in the country. When the economy is in recession, business slows down, unemployment goes up and there are fewer economic activities, with the result that expenditures under those programs automatically increase. That is why they are called stabilizers. So the impact of a recession is that the federal government deficit is bound to grow because revenues are down and some expenditures automatically increase.
Now then, is it sound financial, fiscal and economic management when the government opts for deficit financing during a recession? I for one think so, Mr. Speaker, quite so. First of all, it has been noted that in times of economic doldrums, the savings rate of Canadians rises dramatically. It increases sharply. This year Canadians are setting aside 14 per cent of their income precisely because the economic situation has them worried. When Canadian savings are so high during a period of economic slowdown and all that money is left on deposit with banks, credit unions and trust companies, we cannot expect the private sector to be anxious to use it to spur the economy, if only because in the private sector right now the manufacturing industry, for instance, is operating at barely 55 or 60 per cent of its capacity. Therefore, should we decide to leave these funds in Canadian banks or in the Caisses Populaires, and should the government not borrow any money, no one is assured that this money will really be used to stimulate the economy in order to meet the needs of those groups in our society or in the economy who need attention the most. I think it is wise for the government, as a matter of economic policy, to get involved in the marketplace in times such as those, to grow a deficit and to borrow, because this will stimulate the economy.
In the June 28 budget, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Mac-Eachen) proposed to allocate funds to specific areas: housing, through a $3,000 grant to people who will build or buy their first home, direct job-creation programs, on which more than $400 million will be spent, economic development projects for which $300 million will be earmarked; in addition, the government will consider setting up a permanent and structural change within our interest rates policies in order to ensure that small businesses, home owners with mortgage payments, farmers and fishermen will get loans at an interest rate from 3 to 6 percent lower than usual. This will enable the government to redistribute the wealth of our country. By not adopting a high deficit policy in times of recession, I think we would delay

economic recovery because we must ensure that helpless people are not the only ones to bear the brunt of an economic recession. The federal and provincial governments have the responsibility to find means of stabilizing and reducing the social costs of economic slowdowns.
In addition, Mr. Speaker, I think the government should not be reluctant to resort to what is called deficit financing, even in times of economic recovery, because a government debt is like an individual debt. We should consider that over the past and present years the government has built up funds that will be made available for public services for years to come. Why then should the wage-earners of 1982 be the only ones to pay for those services through their taxes? I think it is reasonable, Mr. Speaker, to expect the people who will be using those services
later to pay their share and this is why I feel we are entitled to borrow.
Therefore Mr. Speaker, I think that the Leader of the Opposition's amendment to restrain the government's borrowing power is absolutely useless and would merely result in our having to introduce another bill in the fall. It is only intended to hinder the financial planning of the government, and accordingly I will vote against the amendment.
